Minimum Wage Increases, Wages, and Low-Wage Employment: Evidence from Seattle

This paper evaluates the wage, hours and employment effects of the second phase of Seattle's minimum wage ordinance, which raised the minimum wage from $11 to $13 per hour in 2016, using administrative records covering all workers in the state.

The increase to $13 reduced hours worked in low-wage jobs by around 9 percent, while hourly wages in such jobs increased by around 3 percent. Consequently, total payroll fell for such jobs, implying that the minimum wage ordinance lowered low-wage employees' earnings by an average of $125 per month in 2016.

Evidence attributes more modest effects to the first wage increase, to $11, and we discuss how our estimates relate to the broader literature on local minimum wages and the limits of a single-city analysis.
